chapter_theme: Love cannot be hidden, gives itself away to the bone, and is what makes a body alive. Without it, virtue burns a person and a life is a withered tree.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar divides the chapter: love's reality (71), its excellence (72-76), and the fault of lacking it (77-80). The verses also keep rhyming அன்பு with என்பு, love with bone (72, 73, 77, 80), and this runs through the chapter as its sound and argument.

71.reading: Is there any bolt that can shut in even love? The small tears of the loving will proclaim it.
71.nuance: A tiny tear (புன்கணீர்) produces an uproar (பூசல்), and the contrast in scale is the point. Parimelazhagar specifies that the tears fall at the beloved's pain, and he treats them as logical inference: love is unseen but can be inferred.

72.reading: The loveless belong to themselves in everything, and the loving belong to others even to their bones.
72.nuance: Love is framed as a question of ownership. Parimelazhagar glosses the bones by citing Purananuru 43, on the king who gave his own flesh for a dove, which is a direct thread to the Sangam corpus.

73.reading: They say the bond of the precious life with the bone is the way that came to be joined with love.
73.nuance: The syntax is compressed, and the verse could give embodiment a purpose or a past cause. On Parimelazhagar's reading, the body exists for loving, which is an unusually positive view of embodiment. Pope's gloss follows the past-birth view.

positions.position: The soul is joined to a body for the purpose of love, since love can't be done without one.
positions.quote: உடம்போடு இயைந்தல்லது அன்பு செய்யலாகாமையின், அது செய்தற் பொருட்டு இத்தொடர்ச்சி உளதாயிற்று

positions.position: The present embodiment results from love practised in a previous birth.
positions.quote: முற்பிறப்பின்கண் அன்போடு பொருந்தச் சென்ற செலவென்று சொல்லுவர்

positions.position: The verse is an analogy: love and action should fit as soul and body do.

74.reading: Love gives rise to eagerness for others, and that gives rise to the unsought distinction called friendship.
74.nuance: Love is a seed with a sequence. Parimelazhagar widens the final term a great deal: love for one's own extends to everyone, until the person has neither enemies nor neutrals. நாடா, unsought, suggests this distinction arrives without being chased.

75.reading: They say that the distinction won by those who have known joy in this world is the outcome of a life settled in love.
75.nuance: The commentators disagree about the timeline. Manakkudavar puts the love in a past birth, Parimelazhagar puts the distinction in heaven after this life, and Kalaignar keeps both in this life. Parimelazhagar's contrast is a pointed one: ascetics reach heaven through pain, while householders reach it through joy.

76.reading: The ignorant say that love supports only virtue, but it is also the ally against, or of, மறம்.
76.nuance: The word மறம் is the problem. It can mean sin or valour, and the ambiguous dative 'for மறம்' leaves open whether love helps to remove it or to do it.

positions.position: மறம் is hostile feeling, and love helps remove it when one treats an enemy as a friend.
Love also stands by those who do மறம்.
மறம் is heroism, and heroic action is also backed by love.

77.reading: Virtue burns what has no love, as the sun burns what has no bones.
77.nuance: It is a chilling image, and on Parimelazhagar's explanation the sun bears no malice: it shines equally, and the boneless creature perishes by its own nature. Virtue is thus not vindictive, which makes this verse more unsettling.

positions.position: This is அறம் personified as a deity, impersonal like the sun, and the loveless soul perishes before it.
What burns is one's own conscience, in someone who knows virtue but doesn't follow it.

78.reading: A life without love inside is like a dried tree putting forth shoots on hard ground.
78.nuance: The image is an impossibility, as Parimelazhagar says and as Manakkudavar explains: there is nothing in the tree to cause sprouting. The verse says உயிர்வாழ்க்கை, a living being's life, and Parimelazhagar and Pope narrow it to household life.

79.reading: What use are all the outer parts to those without love, the inner part of the body?
79.nuance: Love is classed as an organ, which is a striking way to make it non-optional. Parimelazhagar explicitly refutes the bodily-organs reading that Kalaignar's comment follows.

positions.position: Outer 'parts' are household means such as place, wealth and servants, because the body reading has no connection to household life.
positions.quote: புறத்து உறுப்பாவன: இடனும், பொருளும், ஏவல் செய்வாரும் முதலாயின.

positions.position: Outer parts are the body's beauty, which is pointless without love.

80.reading: The seat of life goes by way of love; for those without it, a body is bones wrapped in skin.
80.nuance: The final verse is about what counts as alive, and it isn't an exaggeration about ethics. Manakkudavar connects உயிர்நிலை to release, whereas Parimelazhagar connects it to the household virtue that makes a body live.

links.note: Both say that a living body can be dead in effect, and Manakkudavar on 9 also says such bodies lack life. The criterion is worship in chapter 1 and love in chapter 8, so the two chapters compete for what makes a person alive.

Both picture a bolted door. Love has no bolt here, and in 1251 desire breaks the door of நிறை that shame has barred. The image passes from the ethics of love to its erotic form, with the same result: it won't stay shut in.
This strengthens Kalaignar's reading of 76. In 773, the highest courage is fierce, and its sharp edge is kindness to those in need, so the book elsewhere does join courage to kindness.
